title: Sunderland reach deal to sell majority stake in women’s team
content:
Sunderland have reached an agreement to sell a significant majority stake in their women’s team to Bay Collective, the multi-club ownership group backed by Sixth Street, a U.S. private investment firm.

Specifics of the deal have not been disclosed but multiple sources with knowledge of the discussions, speaking on condition of anonymity to protect relationships, confirmed to The Athletic Bay Collective will acquire a holding in the region of 80 per cent, pending approval from WSL Football, which oversees the top two divisions of women’s football in England. That 80 per cent figure mirrors reporting from Bloomberg in late March.

The Athletic exclusively revealed Bay Collective as a potential buyer at the end of February, and confirmed discussions between the two parties were ongoing even as a period of exclusivity came to an end.

Bay Collective is headed by Kay Cossington, the English FA’s former women’s technical director who was in charge when England won the European Championship in 2022.

The deal will make Sunderland the fourth club in the Premier League to sell a stake in their women’s team to outside investors within the past two years, though this deal is missing one important element from the others.

At each of Chelsea, Aston Villa and Everton, internal restructures of women’s teams were undertaken before then selling stakes to outside investors. Those restructures crystallised gains which contributed positively to the men’s teams’ domestic profitability and sustainability (PSR) calculations, most notoriously at Chelsea. There, in June 2024, the internal ‘sale’ of Chelsea Women to a fellow group company generated a £198million (now $262m) paper profit which, in turn, enabled the men’s team to lose an English record £262m last season without breaching PSR.

By contrast, no such internal ‘sale’ has taken place on Wearside. Sunderland Association Football Club Limited, the men’s team entity, will retain a minority stake in Sunderland Association Football Club Women Limited. The new controlling entity of Sunderland Women is expected to be Bay Collective UK Limited, a UK-registered entity which was set up in April 2025 and of which Cossington is the sole current director.

The price paid is yet to be made public but a source told The Athletic the deal is expected to represent the most significant transaction relating to a WSL2 team. Mercury 13, another multi-club organisation focused on women’s football, acquired a majority stake in Bristol City Women, another second-tier side, in November 2025.

The transaction will generate profit in Sunderland’s men’s team accounts, though that is viewed by the club as an ancillary benefit rather than the main motive behind the sale.

Despite a sizeable transfer spend last summer following promotion to the Premier League, Sunderland are not expected to have any trouble complying with PSR this season.

Combined pre-tax losses over the past two seasons total just £12.6m, with £8m able to be deducted across infrastructure and women’s team spending. Take off other allowable costs on the club’s category one academy and community expenditure and Sunderland’s PSR position was almost certainly profitable heading into 2025-26, meaning the club would have to lose a huge sum this season to be in breach.

That is extremely unlikely given the revenue increase Premier League status brings, and any longer-term benefits of women’s team sales for PSR purposes have been neutered. After this season, Premier League clubs will adhere to a squad cost rule (SCR) which takes no heed of clubs selling such ‘assets’.

The sale to a group with financial backing from Sixth Street is intended to build on progress seen at Sunderland Women since club chairman Kyril Louis-Dreyfus arrived on Wearside in February 2021. Expenditure on the women’s team had dropped to near-zero under Madrox Partners, an entity ran by Stewart Donald, Charlie Methven and Juan Sartori, who remains a shareholder at the club.

In the 2024-25 season, £1.4m was spent on the women’s team, a third more than a season prior, and club support for the team has improved markedly since the club’s ownership change five years ago. Even so, Sunderland Women will remain a WSL2 club in 2026-27, and have not played in the top tier since 2017-18. They were relegated then for failing to apply for a license to play in the WSL.

Speaking alongside Tuesday’s announcement, Cossington described Bay Collective’s arrival on Wearside as “a partnership for the long-term”, and outlined an ambition to create “a platform for sustained success at the highest levels of the women’s game.” With Sixth Street’s financial backing, the group intends to provide Sunderland Women with “cutting-edge resources, infrastructure, and training models tailored to the unique needs of women athletes.”

The long-term nature of the deal was echoed by Tom Burwell, a Sunderland director. He said the agreement “reflects a shared ambition to see our women’s team thrive at the highest level.” Burwell’s primary role is chief executive officer of Bia Sports Group, a firm set up by Louis-Dreyfus and Sartori to manage their sporting investments. He is currently serving as Sunderland’s interim CEO following a recent internal restructure at the club.

What the proceeds from the stake sale will be used for is unknown at this stage.

Strengthening and funding Sunderland Women to the level required to achieve promotion and compete in WSL1 is a stated aim, and investment into the club’s Academy of Light training ground, where the women’s team also operate from, is expected. Sunderland Women’s current costs are around seven times lower than the WSL1 average.

Whether increased funding comes from the sale proceeds, subsequent investment by Bay Collective, or a mix of the two is unclear. Sunderland’s men’s team has been run carefully during a recent period of success but has, like most English clubs, relied on extra funding, which the sale proceeds could potentially replace or repay.

At the end of July 2025, Sunderland owed £19.8m to parent company Mercator Investments, owned by Louis-Dreyfus and Sartori, and a further £25.2m to Akira BV, a Dutch entity within the wider Louis-Dreyfus group of companies which has taken over from Mercator in providing funds.

Reaching an agreement marks the end of a one-year process of evaluating investment options for Sunderland Women, and the intent is to return the club to the top tier. Funding has increased under Louis-Dreyfus but last season’s level of expenditure was still one of the lowest in the WSL.

Of the 17 clubs in last season’s WSL1 and WSL2 for whom spending figures are publicly available, Sunderland’s expenditure was the smallest, though five clubs have not disclosed detailed financials.

Assuming WSL approval is granted, Sunderland will become the second club in Bay Collective’s group. Sixth Street paid a then-record $53m franchise fee for San Francisco-based Bay FC to join the National Women’s Soccer League in 2023, and has invested more into the club since. A spokesperson for Sixth Street said the investment in Sunderland Women is “a continuation of Sixth Street’s long-term growth investments in women’s sports.”

Bay Collective is the U.S. firm’s main foray into women’s football, but it follows two high-profile deals carried out by the firm in the men’s game, totalling almost €1bn.

Sixth Street purchased a proportion of the future proceeds from Real Madrid’s revamped Bernabeu home for €327m in the 2021-22 season, around the same time it acquired a quarter of Barcelona’s future domestic TV money for €667.5m.
